summary: Once-daily antidepressant for major depressive disorder (MDD) that combines SSRI activity with 5-HT1A partial agonism. Must be taken with food for full effect. Common early side effects are nausea and diarrhea.
description: Vilazodone is a daily antidepressant for adults with major depression. It works on serotonin in two ways (SSRI + 5-HT1A partial agonist). Most people notice early changes in 1-2 weeks, with fuller improvement building over 4-6 weeks. GI side effects (especially diarrhea and nausea) are common early on. Take it with food—taking it on an empty stomach can cut absorption in about half and make it feel like it’s “not working.” Like all antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts/behavior in young people and requires close monitoring during the first 1-2 months and after dose changes.
patient_summary: Vilazodone (Viibryd) is a once-daily antidepressant for adults with major depression. It has a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts/behavior in young people, so early monitoring matters. It commonly causes diarrhea, nausea, and headache—especially early. Take it with food every time; fasting can reduce levels by ~50% and lower the benefit.

primary.context: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder (unipolar depression) in adults. Typically assessed over 4-6 weeks for meaningful response, with earlier shifts (sleep, appetite, energy, reactivity) sometimes showing up in 1-2 weeks.

therapeutic_response.display: Initial effects may be observed within 1-2 weeks; continued improvement through 4-6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the signature vilazodone side effect early on. It often improves with time. Taking with food helps tolerability and also helps the medication absorb properly.
Usually shows up early, especially if taken without enough food. If nausea is intense, slow down the titration plan and get consistent with meals.
Often early and can settle down. Hydration, sleep regularity, and avoiding missed doses can help.
More likely during dose increases or if you miss doses and restart. Stand up slowly and flag persistent dizziness to your prescriber.
Some people get insomnia or vivid dreams. If sleep worsens, discuss timing of the dose and sleep hygiene before assuming the medication is a failure.
Vilazodone isn’t typically a heavy sedator, but some people feel tired or foggy early. If it persists, reassess dose and timing.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Decreased libido 2% to 4%; erectile dysfunction 3%; abnormal orgasm 1% to 2%
common_adverse_effects.notes: Sexual side effects can happen even if mood improves. Don’t suffer in silence—there are workarounds (dose timing, adjuncts, or switching strategies).

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal ideation or suicidal tendencies (especially early in treatment or after dose changes): urgent evaluation required
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, delirium, fever, sweating, tremor, rigidity, diarrhea, seizures—medical emergency
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, risky behavior, grandiosity, racing thoughts—stop and reassess for bipolar disorder
Hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, headache, weakness, falls; can be severe in older adults
Bleeding complications: bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding—higher risk with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants
Acute pancreatitis (postmarketing): severe abdominal pain, vomiting—seek urgent care
Severe allergic reactions (postmarketing): rash, urticaria; stop and seek care if severe

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Vilazodone is not approved for use in pediatric patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) concurrently or within 14 days of discontinuing either vilazodone or the MAOI
Use with IV methylene blue (an MAOI) concurrently or within 14 days
Hypersensitivity to vilazodone or any component of the formulation (noted in Canadian labeling)

precautions: Serotonin syndrome can be life-threatening, especially when combined with other serotonergic drugs or MAOIs
Bleeding risk increases when combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents
Mania/hypomania can be triggered in people with bipolar disorder—screen before starting; antidepressant monotherapy is risky in bipolar
Hyponatremia/SIADH can occur, especially in older adults or those on diuretics
Narrow-angle glaucoma risk due to pupillary dilation in susceptible individuals
Discontinuation syndrome can occur if stopped abruptly—taper when appropriate
Seizure risk: use caution in patients with seizure disorders or conditions that lower seizure threshold

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated: high risk of serotonin syndrome.
interactions.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting vilazodone, and 14 days between stopping vilazodone and starting an MAOI.

interactions.mechanism: Manufacturer labeling lists as contraindicated, but newer evidence suggests serotonin syndrome risk is low and may be manageable with monitoring in necessary cases.
interactions.action: If coadministration is truly necessary, monitor closely for serotonin toxicity and educate on symptoms. Escalate care if concerning signs appear.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, TCAs, lithium, tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, buspirone, amphetamines, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
interactions.action: Avoid unnecessary stacking. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely, especially during starts and dose changes.

interactions.interactant: NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents (e.g., warfarin)
interactions.mechanism: Increased bleeding risk due to impaired platelet aggregation.
interactions.action: Use caution, watch for bruising/nosebleeds/black stools, and coordinate monitoring when clinically indicated.

interactions.mechanism: Can raise vilazodone levels and increase side effects.
interactions.action: Dose/frequency adjustment may be required depending on the inhibitor and clinical situation.

interactions.mechanism: Can lower vilazodone levels and reduce antidepressant effect.
interactions.action: Avoid if possible; if unavoidable, monitor for loss of response and consider alternative strategy.

interactions.mechanism: May worsen dizziness, sedation, and judgment impairment in some people.
interactions.action: If you drink, keep it minimal and be honest about it—especially early, when side effects are still settling.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Depression symptoms and functional recovery: track mood, motivation, sleep, appetite, concentration, and day-to-day functioning over 4-6 weeks using a validated tool when possible.
Suicidal ideation and behavior: monitor closely during the first 1-2 months and during dose increases or decreases; involve family/caregivers when appropriate.
Activation, anxiety, agitation, panic, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia/restlessness: these can signal intolerance or emerging risk and should be reported quickly.
Mania/hypomania: screen for bipolar disorder before starting and monitor for mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and risky behavior.
Serotonin syndrome: watch especially when combined with other serotonergic agents; monitor for agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor/rigidity, diarrhea, and seizures.
Hyponatremia/SIADH: monitor sodium closely when initiating or adjusting in older adults and those on diuretics or with volume depletion; watch for confusion, weakness, headaches, and falls.
Bleeding: monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding signs, especially if combined with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants.
Sexual function: decreased libido, orgasm changes, erectile dysfunction—track because it affects adherence and quality of life.
GI tolerability: diarrhea/nausea early; ensure consistent dosing with food and reassess titration speed if needed.

special_populations.pregnancy: Outcome data in pregnancy are limited. Like other SSRIs, late-pregnancy exposure may be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome and a rare risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Reducing the dose or stopping close to delivery to prevent neonatal adaptation syndrome is not recommended. SSRIs may be associated with a small increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Untreated or undertreated depression is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and relapse risk rises when effective treatment is discontinued. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible and monitor symptoms monthly with a validated tool during pregnancy.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if vilazodone is present in breast milk, and postpartum data are limited. Infants exposed to SSRIs via breast milk should be monitored for irritability, changes in sleep/feeding, behavior changes, growth, and development. If initiating an antidepressant for the first time while breastfeeding, an agent with more lactation data may be preferred; however, treatment should not be withheld solely due to breastfeeding status.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients; monitoring is especially important early in treatment and after dose changes.
special_populations.geriatric: Use with caution in adults ≥65 due to risk of SIADH/hyponatremia (Beers Criteria: use with caution and monitor sodium when initiating or adjusting). Older adults may also be more vulnerable to dizziness and falls if hyponatremia develops.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Food-dependent; taking without food can reduce exposure by ~50%
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 (major) and CYP2C19/CYP2D6 (minor); no known active metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Fasted state can decrease concentrations by ~50%; administer with food

dosing.titration: Vilazodone is dosed once daily and titrated up to reduce side effects. Take it with food every time—fasted dosing can drop drug exposure by ~50% and reduce benefit.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you’ve been on vilazodone regularly for 4 weeks or more, tapering reduces the odds of discontinuation symptoms (nausea, dizziness, irritability, sleep disruption, vivid dreams, “brain zaps,” anxiety, mood swings). The more sensitive your system (or the longer you’ve been on it), the slower the taper should be.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Vilazodone (Viibryd) is used to treat {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder (MDD)} in adults. It’s not a “knock-you-out” med or an as-needed anxiety pill—it’s a daily antidepressant meant to build benefit over weeks. The biggest practical rule: take it with food every time, or the medication level can drop a lot and the results can get shaky.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, changes in sleep/appetite, low energy, guilt, concentration problems, and/or suicidal thoughts
Depression with prominent anxiety symptoms: Not a separate FDA indication, but often chosen when depression comes with agitation, worry, and rumination

sections.heading: What People Feel

items.category: Week 1-2: Stomach stuff (the classic start-up phase)
quotes: Day one hit me with nausea like I’d taken it on an empty stomach… because I did.
The diarrhea was real at first, then it calmed down.
I learned fast: if I don’t eat with it, I feel it—and not in a good way.
items.note: GI side effects (especially diarrhea and nausea) are common early on. Taking it with food helps both absorption and tolerability.

quotes: It wasn’t instant, but I realized I was crying less and doing more.
The volume on the dark thoughts turned down gradually.
I didn’t feel numb—just less trapped.
items.note: Early changes can show up in sleep, energy, reactivity, and motivation before mood fully lifts.

items.category: Activation vs sedation (it’s not a “sleeping pill” antidepressant)
quotes: I felt a little wired at night at first—had to adjust my routine.
Not sedating. If anything, it pushed me to be more awake.
Sleep got weird for a bit: vivid dreams and restless nights.
items.note: Some people feel insomnia, restlessness, or akathisia-like inner jitter early, especially during titration.

items.category: Sexual side effects (yes, they still happen)
quotes: Libido dropped and orgasm got harder—annoying but manageable.
The mood improved faster than my sex life did.
I didn’t expect sexual side effects with this one, but here we are.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction can occur (decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, abnormal orgasm).

quotes: I missed doses and felt dizzy and irritable—like my brain was protesting.
When I tried to quit cold, I got nausea, weird dreams, and mood swings.
Tapering fixed it. Cold turkey was a mistake.
items.note: Discontinuation symptoms can happen with abrupt stopping—tapering is the move, especially after longer use.

sections.intro: Everyone’s experience is different, but vilazodone tends to have a pretty recognizable “pattern,” especially in the first couple weeks:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Vilazodone is not a same-day relief medication. Think weeks, not hours. You may notice early shifts in 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement through weeks 4-6.
key_points: Day 1-7: Side effects often show up before benefits (GI symptoms are common early)
Week 1-2: Some people notice small changes (sleep, appetite, reactivity, energy)
Week 4-6: This is the typical window for clearer antidepressant response
4-5 hours: Time to peak blood level after a dose
Food matters: Taking it without food can reduce levels by ~50%

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Vilazodone can be effective for major depression, but it’s a gradual builder. The most common reason it “fails” in real life is inconsistent dosing with food—if you take it fasting, exposure can drop hard and the benefit can fade. If you’re taking it correctly (daily, with food), the typical plan is to give it several weeks and track functional changes—not just mood.
sections.value: Early shifts in 1-2 weeks; fuller benefit builds over 4-6 weeks
sections.clinical_details: A practical read: vilazodone is once-daily and not sedating for most people. The tradeoff is early GI side effects and the strict requirement to take it with food. Response is monitored over weeks, and dose increases are based on tolerability and symptom movement.

If you plan to stop, don’t yank it. Tapering helps prevent withdrawal symptoms.

sections.intro: Vilazodone is serotonergic and primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. The biggest interaction risks are serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergic drugs/MAOIs) and altered levels with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers. Also: bleeding risk rises when combined with NSAIDs or blood thinners.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on vilazodone regularly for 4 weeks or more, tapering reduces the odds of discontinuation symptoms (nausea, dizziness, irritability, sleep disruption, vivid dreams, “brain zaps,” anxiety, mood swings). The more sensitive your system (or the longer you’ve been on it), the slower the taper should be.
key_points: If taking 40 mg/day and stopping after ≥4 weeks: taper to 20 mg once daily for 4 days, then 10 mg once daily for 3 days.
If taking 20 mg/day and stopping after ≥4 weeks: taper to 10 mg once daily for 7 days.
If treatment was brief (2-3 weeks): taper over 1-2 weeks is often reasonable; <2 weeks often doesn’t require a formal taper, but sensitivity varies.
If withdrawal symptoms are intense: go back to the prior tolerated dose and taper more gradually.
If you have a history of discontinuation syndrome, high doses, or long-term use (>6 months): consider a slower taper (sometimes weeks to months).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Vilazodone is dosed once daily and titrated up to reduce side effects. Take it with food every time—fasted dosing can drop drug exposure by ~50% and reduce benefit.

adult.mdd_initial: 10 mg PO once daily with food for 7 days
adult.mdd_titration: Increase to 20 mg PO once daily with food after 7 days; may increase to 40 mg PO once daily with food after an additional ≥7 days based on response and tolerability
adult.mdd_max: 40 mg/day PO once daily with food
adult.with_food: Administer with food; fasting can decrease concentrations by ~50% and may reduce effect
adult.older_adults: Refer to adult dosing; use extra caution for hyponatremia/SIADH risk and monitor sodium when starting or adjusting

sections.simple_explanation: Vilazodone is a once-daily antidepressant that’s titrated slowly to improve tolerability. The most important practical detail is food: taking it without food can cut absorption dramatically and make the medication feel inconsistent.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy and postpartum decisions should be individualized. The biggest theme here is shared decision-making: untreated depression has real risks, and stopping an effective medication can trigger relapse. Vilazodone has limited pregnancy and breastfeeding data compared with some other SSRIs, so it’s often not first-line when starting fresh—but people who are stable on it may continue if the benefits outweigh the risks.

Untreated or undertreated depression is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and relapse risk rises when effective treatment is discontinued. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible and monitor symptoms monthly with a validated tool during pregnancy.

Starter pack (oral kit): 10 mg & 20 mg (product status may vary by market)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Vilazodone works on serotonin in two ways: it blocks serotonin reuptake (SSRI effect) and partially activates 5-HT1A receptors (5-HT1A partial agonist). In plain language: it increases serotonin signaling and also “tunes” a serotonin receptor that’s involved in mood and anxiety circuitry. That combo is why it’s sometimes described as a serotonin modulator, not just a standard SSRI.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Vilazodone is one of several reasonable antidepressant options for MDD. Clinically, it’s often considered when someone wants a once-daily medication and is okay with the possibility of early GI side effects. It’s not a first-line choice for everyone, especially in pregnancy or breastfeeding when treatment-naive, because data are more limited than for some other SSRIs. The biggest make-or-break practical issue is dosing with food—this medication is unusually sensitive to that.

faqs.a: Vilazodone is used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults. It’s a daily antidepressant—not an as-needed med—and it’s meant to build benefit over weeks.

faqs.q: How long does vilazodone take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes in 1-2 weeks (like sleep, energy, and reactivity), but the more meaningful antidepressant effect usually develops over 4-6 weeks.

faqs.q: Do I really have to take vilazodone with food?
faqs.a: Yes. This one is unusually food-dependent. Taking vilazodone without food can reduce drug exposure by about 50%, which can make it feel less effective or inconsistent.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are diarrhea, nausea, and headache. Dizziness, insomnia, restlessness, fatigue, and sexual side effects can also happen.

faqs.q: Can vilazodone cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: Yes. Sexual dysfunction can occur, including decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and orgasm changes. If it happens, tell your prescriber—there are options to manage it.

faqs.q: Does vilazodone have a suicidality boxed warning?
faqs.a: Yes. Like other antidepressants, vilazodone carries a boxed warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients. Close monitoring is especially important during the first 1-2 months and after dose changes. Vilazodone is not approved for pediatric use.

It can in people with bipolar disorder. Any antidepressant can push someone into hypomania/mania if bipolar is in the background. That’s why screening for bipolar symptoms matters before starting, and why new symptoms like decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, or risky behavior need quick attention.

faqs.q: What drugs should not be combined with vilazodone?
faqs.a: MAOIs are the big contraindication—do not combine, and keep a 14-day window when switching. Also use caution with other serotonergic meds (risk of serotonin syndrome) and with NSAIDs or blood thinners (higher bleeding risk).

faqs.q: What is serotonin syndrome and what should I watch for?
faqs.a: Serotonin syndrome is a rare but potentially life-threatening reaction from too much serotonergic activity, especially when meds are combined. Warning signs include agitation, confusion, fever, heavy sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, diarrhea, fast heart rate, and seizures. Severe symptoms need emergency care.

faqs.q: How do I taper off vilazodone safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or more, tapering helps prevent discontinuation symptoms. A common approach: if on 40 mg/day, step down to 20 mg daily for 4 days, then 10 mg daily for 3 days. If on 20 mg/day, step down to 10 mg daily for 7 days. If you’re sensitive or have had withdrawal before, taper more slowly.

faqs.q: Is vilazodone safe in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Data are limited compared with some other SSRIs, so it’s often not first-line if starting new in pregnancy or breastfeeding. But treatment decisions should be individualized—untreated depression carries real risks, and stopping an effective medication can cause relapse. This is a shared decision-making conversation with your clinician.

faqs.q: What if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: Take the next dose as directed (usually the next day) and avoid doubling up unless your prescriber tells you otherwise. Missing doses can sometimes cause dizziness, irritability, GI symptoms, or sleep disruption—consistent daily dosing with food matters with this medication.
